heading: 1. Community Similarity Tracks Spatial Arrangement at Meter Scale

text: Across nine SSO sediment wells on a 3×3 grid spanning ~6 m, similarity declines with distance (Mantel Spearman ρ = 0.323, p = 0.029; 9,999 permutations). Mean Bray–Curtis dissimilarity is 0.747, ranging from 0.558 to 0.872.
quote: Sediment-associated microbial communities across the 9 SSO wells (3×3 grid, ~6 m span) show significant distance-decay of similarity (Mantel test: Spearman ρ = 0.323, p = 0.029, 9,999 permutations). Mean Bray-Curtis dissimilarity = 0.747, ranging from 0.558 (U3–M6, most similar) to 0.872 (U3–L9, most dissimilar). NMDS ordination achieves low stress (0.067), and Procrustes analysis shows marginal correspondence between community ordination and physical grid (m² = 0.379, p = 0.080).
heading: 1. Community Similarity Tracks Spatial Arrangement at Meter Scale

text: NMDS stress is 0.067, but Procrustes correspondence with the physical grid is marginal (m² = 0.379, p = 0.080).
quote: Sediment-associated microbial communities across the 9 SSO wells (3×3 grid, ~6 m span) show significant distance-decay of similarity (Mantel test: Spearman ρ = 0.323, p = 0.029, 9,999 permutations). Mean Bray-Curtis dissimilarity = 0.747, ranging from 0.558 (U3–M6, most similar) to 0.872 (U3–L9, most dissimilar). heading: 1. Community Similarity Tracks Spatial Arrangement at Meter Scale

text: Uphill–downhill structuring is not supported (Mantel ρ = −0.049, p = 0.580); the east–west association is suggestive but not conventionally significant (ρ = 0.227, p = 0.092).
quote: Critically, community turnover is **not** aligned with the hillslope (uphill-downhill Mantel ρ = −0.049, p = 0.580) but instead with the **east-west axis** (column Mantel ρ = 0.227, p = 0.092). This contradicts the naive expectation of topography-driven hydrology and points to a lateral structuring force.

text: Nitrifiers and iron oxidizers co-occur at U3 (ρ = +0.95), interpreted as plume-entry chemolithotrophs.

text: Syntrophs and fermenters co-occur (ρ = +0.55), interpreted as anaerobic food-web coupling.
quote: - **Syntroph × fermenter**: ρ = +0.55 — classic anaerobic food web coupling. Fermenters produce organic acids and H₂; syntrophs consume these in obligate partnerships with sulfate reducers or methanogens.

text: Denitrifiers and syntrophs are negatively associated (ρ = −0.67), consistent with redox separation.
quote: - **Denitrifier × syntroph**: ρ = −0.67 — mutual exclusion across the redox gradient. Denitrifiers thrive where nitrate is available (oxidizing); syntrophs require strictly anaerobic conditions.
heading: 6. Metabolic Guild Structure and Inferred Interactions

text: Sulfate reducers and aerobic heterotrophs are negatively associated (ρ = −0.75), consistent with redox separation.
quote: - **Sulfate reducer × aerobic heterotroph**: ρ = −0.75 — textbook redox separation. These guilds occupy opposite ends of the electron acceptor hierarchy.

text: A northeast-to-southwest saturated-zone plume is the report's explanatory model, not an independently verified flow-path measurement.
quote: All findings converge on a single explanatory model: **the spatial structure of SSO microbial communities is governed by a contamination plume entering from the northeast and flowing southwest through the saturated zone.**
heading: The Contamination Plume Model

text: The SSO is downhill and southwest of the Oak Ridge Reservation Area 3 contamination source, reported to deliver high-nitrate, low-pH water containing uranium, chromium and nickel.
quote: The SSO sits downhill and southwest of a contamination source at Oak Ridge Reservation Area 3, which delivers high nitrate, low pH water laden with heavy metals (uranium, chromium, nickel). The plume enters the grid near **U3** (upper-east) and flows diagonally toward **L7** (lower-west), creating the **Column 3 corridor** identified in NB02.
heading: The Contamination Plume Model

text: Rhodanobacter is associated with contaminated Oak Ridge Reservation groundwater; the cited literature reports up to 45% of 16S sequences in low-pH, high-nitrate wells, while this project reports 7.7% at M5.
quote: The dominance of *Rhodanobacter* in contaminated ORR groundwater is well-established. Green et al. (2012) showed that *Rhodanobacter* species dominate bacterial communities in the most contaminated zones of the ORR subsurface, accounting for up to 45% of 16S sequences in low-pH, high-nitrate wells. Our finding of 7.7% *Rhodanobacter* at M5 is consistent with moderate plume influence — lower than the most contaminated Area 2 wells but clearly elevated above background.
heading: Literature Context

text: Anaeromyxobacter dehalogenans is described as an ENIGMA model organism for iron and uranium reduction; the report gives 1.3% mean SSO sediment abundance and 41× greater abundance in sediment than groundwater.
quote: *Anaeromyxobacter dehalogenans*, found throughout SSO sediments (1.3% mean), is a model ENIGMA organism for iron and uranium reduction in the ORR subsurface (Thomas et al. 2010). Its enrichment in sediment over groundwater (41× higher in sediment) is consistent with its known biofilm-forming, surface-attached lifestyle.
heading: Literature Context

text: The report compares its 16S amplicon evidence with separate ORR work on 77 sediment and 33 groundwater metagenomes; these are distinct data.
quote: Recent work generating 77 sediment and 33 groundwater metagenomes from the ORR (MRA 2025) examines attached vs planktonic communities — our 16S-based findings provide complementary amplicon-level evidence supporting the same pattern of distinct sediment and groundwater assemblages.
heading: Literature Context

text: Guild co-occurrence is interpreted using prior syntrophic theory and redox zonation; the reported correlations alone do not establish obligate partnerships or causal electron-acceptor separation.
quote: The guild co-occurrence patterns (NB07) are consistent with established syntrophic theory. The tight coupling of syntrophs and fermenters (ρ = +0.55) reflects the thermodynamic interdependence described by McInerney et al. (2009): syntrophic fatty acid degradation requires fermentation products (H₂, acetate, formate) to be maintained at low concentrations, creating obligate partnerships. The mutual exclusion of denitrifiers and syntrophs (ρ = −0.67) maps onto the canonical redox zonation of contaminated aquifers (Chapelle 2001), where electron acceptor availability segregates metabolic guilds spatially.
heading: Literature Context

text: Across groundwater wells sampled 9 days apart, well explained 49.9% of community variation and date explained 0.8%; NB08 refers to the temporal-stability notebook, not a sampling location.
quote: The 9-day temporal stability of groundwater communities (NB08: well R² = 49.9%, date R² = 0.8%)
heading: Literature Context

text: The report maps inferred biogeochemical processes across the SSO 3×3 grid using 16S composition at phylum, class, and genus resolution; the processes were inferred, not directly measured.
quote: This analysis provides the first spatially explicit mapping of biogeochemical process distributions across the SSO 3×3 grid, inferred from 16S community composition at three taxonomic resolutions (phylum, class, genus).
heading: Novel Contribution

text: A U3-M6-L7 community-similarity corridor aligns with the expected NE→SW plume trajectory; this is an inference from Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, not direct hydrological measurement.
quote: 1. **The plume flow path is visible in community similarity**: The U3-M6-L7 corridor, identified purely from Bray-Curtis dissimilarity patterns, aligns with the expected NE→SW plume trajectory — demonstrating that 16S community similarity can map subsurface hydrology at meter scale.
heading: Novel Contribution

text: Genus-based trait inference places the O₂ → NO₃⁻ → Fe(III) → SO₄²⁻ → fermentation sequence and putative process hotspots on the well grid.
quote: 2. **The redox ladder is spatially resolved**: Genus-level functional inference maps the classic thermodynamic electron acceptor sequence (O₂ → NO₃⁻ → Fe(III) → SO₄²⁻ → fermentation) onto the physical grid, with specific process hotspots at specific wells.
heading: Novel Contribution

text: The report proposes M5 as a nitrate–organic-carbon mixing zone from a denitrification-associated Rhodanobacter peak of 7.7%; geochemical validation remains pending.
quote: 3. **M5 as the mixing zone**: The central well's denitrification peak (*Rhodanobacter* at 7.7%) identifies the precise location where plume nitrate meets background organic carbon — a prediction that can be validated when SSO geochemistry data is loaded into CORAL.
heading: Novel Contribution

text: Vertical community zonation has PERMANOVA R² = 27.5%; the report interprets it as plume confinement to the saturated zone and reports no contamination effect above the water table, without direct geochemical confirmation.
quote: 4. **Depth × plume interaction**: The vertical zonation (PERMANOVA R² = 27.5%) reflects the plume's confinement to the saturated zone, not just generic depth gradients. Above the water table, communities are unaffected by contamination.
heading: Novel Contribution

text: Inferred guild abundances show nitrifier–iron-oxidizer correlation ρ = +0.95 and denitrifier–syntroph correlation ρ = −0.67; mechanistic interpretation remains based on co-occurrence.
quote: 5. **Guild co-occurrence maps the metabolic network**: The strong nitrifier-iron oxidizer coupling (ρ = +0.95) and denitrifier-syntroph exclusion (ρ = −0.67) provide a functional network topology that overlays the spatial redox gradient — connecting community composition to biogeochemical mechanism.
heading: Novel Contribution

heading: Limitations

text: Genus-level functional annotation covers 21% of total reads and 65 of 1,038 genera; inferred process abundances are lower bounds, and 56% unclassified reads may contain further functional capacity.
quote: - **Genus coverage uncertainty**: Genus-level functional annotation covers only 21% of total reads (65 of 1,038 genera). Process abundance estimates are lower bounds; the unclassified 56% of reads could harbor additional functional capacity.
heading: Limitations

text: Class-level traits cover 78% and show consistent redox patterns, but a formal sensitivity comparison with genus-level patterns is still needed.
quote: Sensitivity to this coverage gap should be assessed by comparing genus-level patterns with the higher-coverage class-level traits (78%), which show consistent redox patterns.
heading: Limitations

text: Species classification is ~0%, genus classification covers 44% of sediment reads, and function is assigned from literature-based traits rather than population genomes.
quote: - **Taxonomy resolution**: Species-level classification is ~0%; genus-level covers only 44% of sediment reads. Functional inference relies on literature-based trait assignments rather than direct genomic evidence.
heading: Limitations

text: A single sediment-core sampling event cannot establish temporal plume or community dynamics.
quote: - **Single timepoint for sediment**: Temporal dynamics of the plume and community response cannot be assessed from one core sampling event.
heading: Limitations

text: Phylum- and class-level trait scores are consensus estimates, not measurements of these populations.
quote: - **Trait dictionary subjectivity**: Phylum/class-level trait scores are consensus estimates, not empirical measurements for these specific populations.
heading: Limitations

text: Testable prediction: nitrate, pH, and metals should form a NE→SW gradient, highest at U3/M6 and lowest at M4/U1; this has not been confirmed by loaded SSO geochemistry.
quote: 1. **SSO geochemistry** (when loaded into CORAL): NO₃⁻ concentration, pH, and metal levels should show a NE→SW gradient, with highest contamination at U3/M6 and lowest at M4/U1.
heading: Testable Predictions

text: Testable prediction: EU/ED well-metal data from 100WS/27WS bricks, 90–120 m NE of SSO, should show concentrations decreasing toward SSO.
quote: 2. **Nearby EU/ED well metals** (100WS/27WS bricks, 90–120 m NE of SSO): Should confirm that the contamination plume approaches from the northeast, with metal concentrations decreasing toward the SSO.
heading: Testable Predictions

text: Testable prediction: pump-test groundwater from Bricks 460-462 should show Rhodanobacter highest at M5 versus L8 and U2.
quote: 3. **Pump test groundwater** (Brick 460-462, wells L8/M5/U2): *Rhodanobacter* should be highest at M5 (mixing zone) and lower at L8 and U2.
heading: Testable Predictions

text: Testable prediction: 18 isolate genomes from M6-C2 should encode fermentation or sulfate reduction; this genomic confirmation is not reported here.
quote: 4. **SSO isolate genomes** (18 genomes from M6-C2): Should encode anaerobic metabolisms (fermentation, sulfate reduction) consistent with M6's position in the plume core.
heading: Testable Predictions

text: Loading measurements from 221 registered geochemistry samples—metals, IC/TOC, isotopes, and NH₃/NO₂—would permit direct tests of the plume model.
quote: 1. **Load SSO geochemistry into CORAL**: The 221 registered geochemistry samples (metals, IC/TOC, isotopes, NH₃/NO₂) would allow direct correlation of community composition with measured environmental parameters, validating or refuting the plume model.
heading: Future Directions

text: A proposed Mar 2024 pump-test ASV snapshot from Bricks 460-462 at L8, M5, and U2 could test the M5 denitrification-hotspot prediction.
quote: 2. **Extract pump test ASV data** (Brick 460-462): A third temporal snapshot (Mar 2024) from L8, M5, U2 would test the M5 denitrification hotspot prediction and add temporal resolution.
heading: Future Directions

text: Weighted UniFrac analysis of 16S sequences from Bricks 457/460/477 is proposed as a possible, not demonstrated, improvement over Bray-Curtis for detecting plume effects.
quote: 3. **UniFrac analysis with ASV sequences**: The actual 16S sequences (Bricks 457/460/477) could enable phylogenetic distance-based beta-diversity (weighted UniFrac), which may be more sensitive to plume effects than Bray-Curtis on ASV counts.
heading: Future Directions

text: Spatially matched shotgun metagenomics is proposed to test trait-based functional inference and address the 56% of reads lacking genus-level classification.
quote: 4. **Metagenomics**: Shotgun metagenomics at the same spatial resolution would confirm functional inferences that are currently based on taxonomy-to-trait mapping, and would capture the 56% of reads without genus-level classification.
heading: Future Directions

text: Repeated seasonal 16S profiling is needed to determine whether community structure tracks plume fluctuations.
quote: 5. **Temporal monitoring**: Repeat 16S profiling across seasons and plume dynamics would reveal whether community structure tracks plume fluctuations in real time.
heading: Future Directions
